summary: The note describes the one-child policy, a population planning policy of China that was part of its family planning policy. It was introduced in 1979 after a decade-long two-child policy, loosened in the mid-1980s for rural parents whose first child was a daughter, and eliminated near the end of 2015. The note also covers exceptions for groups including ethnic minorities, provincial fines for violations, and the commissions that handled awareness, registration and inspection. The text is duplicated, and one sentence about girls is truncated and unclear, so it is not summarized.
one_line: China's one-child population policy, introduced in 1979, loosened in the mid-1980s and phased out around the end of 2015.
key_facts: The one-child policy was a part of China's family planning policy and was a population planning policy of China.
The one-child policy was introduced in 1979, after a decade-long two-child policy.
The policy was modified in the mid-1980s to allow rural parents a second child if the first was a daughter.
The policy lasted three more decades before being eliminated near the end of 2015.
The policy began to be formally phased out near the end of 2015 and the beginning of 2016.
The policy was only enforced on Han Chinese.
The policy allowed exceptions for many groups, including ethnic minorities.
In 2007, 36% of China's population was subject to a strict one-child restriction.
Provincial governments imposed fines for violations of the one-child policy.
The local and national governments created commissions to raise awareness and carry out registration and inspection work.
